QF.id: AIFM CII Legal Documents and Negotiations_10

question.text: To avoid breaching fiduciary duty to other investors while granting differential rights to large LPs via side letters, most investment managers follow which drafting practice?

answer.text: They refuse to enter into any side letter, regardless of LP size.
They file each side letter individually with SEBI within 7 days of execution.
They create a separate class of units with differential rights, issued to large investors.
They get written consent from every existing LP before executing any side letter.

explanation.text: The Logic: To avoid a breach of fiduciary duty while still providing differential rights to large investors, the workbook explains that most investment managers create a separate class of units with differential rights and issue those units to the large investors. The class-level terms are then disclosed in the PPM, replacing opaque bilateral side letters with a transparent class structure. The Trap: A blanket refusal of side letters is not the workbook's prescription. There is no rule requiring per-side-letter SEBI filing within 7 days, and universal existing-LP consent is not the drafting mechanism described. Note: When the question asks how managers reconcile differential rights with fiduciary duty, the workbook's answer is always the separate class of units approach disclosed through the PPM.
